text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementNeuroscienceLSD May Speed Up Brain Activity and Make it FractalNew study suggests a more complex reshuffling of experienceKFBy Kristen French3:00 PM CDT on October 22, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleLSD was a relative latecomer to long-established traditions of humans consuming hallucinogenic substances. But in a linguistic sense, it was the first psychedelic. In 1956, British psychiatrist Humphry Osmond coined the term “psychedelic” to describe LSD’s intoxicating effects in correspondence with writer Aldous Huxley. Those who ingest the drug can experience kaleidoscopic visual patterns, a temporary dissolution of self, a slowing or stopping of time, and wild shifts in mood that can range from deep euphoria to severe anxiety and confusion. “To fathom Hell or soar angelic, Just take a pinch of psychedelic,” Osmond quipped in his letter to Huxley.Powered By 10 ShareNextStayRead more: “This Obscure 1960s Guide to LSD Holds Up”Since at least 2012, scientists have believed that LSD and other psychedelics such as psilocybin alter experience by turning the dial down on activity in the brain’s specific control centers, such as the default mode network, which serves as a central conductor, regulating self-reflection and autobiographical memory and maintaining a sense of ego, or self. More recent research has complicated this idea somewhat, suggesting that connections between some networks are actually strengthened by psychedelics.Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
